summary: Describes requirements for SIP telephony devices, drawing on experience with large numbers of SIP phones and PC clients. The aim is interoperable core features so buying and setting up phones is as easy as other devices. It includes a glossary of common settings. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A checklist of what a SIP phone must do, so a phone from any brand works the same and is easy to set up.

questions: what must a sip phone support
subtitle: A checklist of features SIP devices must support for universal compatibility.

tldr.problem: SIP phones from different manufacturers work differently, making it hard for networks to buy phones with confidence and for users to switch devices without losing functionality.
tldr.mechanism: This document lists a common set of interoperable features that all SIP devices should support: network configuration, call handling, security, media negotiation, and device management.
tldr.outcome: Provides vendors and operators with clear guidance on what features to implement, enabling SIP phones to be as easy to buy and use as traditional phones, PCs, and mobile devices.

facts.label: Primary focus
facts.value: Desktop phones and special-purpose SIP devices

today: RFC 4504 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted. It remains widely referenced by SIP device vendors and service providers as the baseline for device interoperability. The requirements have held up well over two decades of SIP deployment, though some features such as video and instant messaging have evolved beyond what this document specifies.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SIP telephony devices—phones, software clients, adapters, and conference units that support the Session Initiation Protocol—are complex devices that must speak many Internet protocols, manage audio and video, and serve different audiences: end users, network administrators, manufacturers, and system integrators. This document specifies requirements for SIP devices based on real-world deployment experience with large numbers of SIP phones in carrier networks, private IP networks, and the Internet.

The goal is simple but important: define a well-supported set of core features so that purchasing, installing, and operating SIP phones is as straightforward as buying a traditional phone, PC, or mobile phone. Without such a standard baseline, networks struggle with compatibility, and vendors must implement diverging feature sets.
sections.eli5: SIP phones are complicated machines. This document says what every SIP phone must do so all phones work the same way.

sections.title: Network and Protocol Foundations
sections.content:
Every SIP device must acquire IP network settings either through automatic configuration via DHCP or manual entry. Devices must support the Simple Network Time Protocol for accurate time, and they must be able to query and cache DNS responses efficiently using multiple configured DNS servers for redundancy. The Device must also support RFC 3263 for locating SIP servers and selecting transport protocols, and many devices should support ENUM for telephone number lookup.

All devices must implement core SIP as specified in RFC 3261, and must be upgradeable so that firmware can be updated either by the user or pushed remotely by a service provider. These network foundations ensure that SIP phones can be deployed in diverse environments and remain functional as the network evolves.
sections.eli5: A SIP phone needs to know its IP address, find the right server to talk to, and keep itself up to date. These are the first rules.

sections.title: Telephony Features and Call Handling
sections.content:
SIP devices must support the basic operations that people expect from a phone: placing a call on hold and taking another call, call waiting indicators that alert users to incoming calls while busy, and call transfer in both attended and unattended modes. Devices must support SIP REFER and NOTIFY for call transfer, send dual-tone multi-frequency (DTMF) telephone events, and handle multiple simultaneous early dialogs during call setup when a call is forked to multiple targets.

Additional features enhance usability: devices should support message waiting notifications to alert users to voicemail, must be able to render reason codes from call failures in the user's language, and may support music on hold and call parking. Support for local dial plans allows devices to transform user input into different URI formats, enabling flexible numbering schemes and international calling.
sections.eli5: A phone must handle calls going on hold, alert you to other callers, and let you transfer calls. It must also dial properly and tell you why a call failed.

sections.title: Security, Quality of Service, and Media
sections.content:
Devices must support digest authentication and Transport Layer Security for secure communication with registrars and proxies, protect configuration from unauthorized access with passwords, and allow administrators to disable unnecessary remote services like SNMP and HTTP. Security also includes the ability to reject calls from unknown senders and to validate that calls come from authorized proxies. Devices must support QoS by marking RTP packets with the appropriate Differentiated Services Code Point for expedited forwarding, and SIP packets with lower priority.

For media, devices must negotiate codecs using the offer-answer model, preferring the first matching codec from the receiver. Implementations should support G.711 (the standard telephone codec) and Internet Low Bit Rate Codec (iLBC), with optional support for mobile codecs, G.729, and specialized codecs like Speex. Devices must comply with voice quality standards for comfort noise, handset receive levels, and echo cancellation.
sections.eli5: A phone must keep calls private with encryption, mark important calls as urgent so the network doesn't drop them, pick a codec that the other phone understands, and sound clear.

sections.title: Device Management and User Mobility
sections.content:
Devices should offer a web interface on a built-in server that lets users manage their phones without special software—configuring settings, building address books, customizing speed dials and ring tones, and setting call handling rules. This same web interface should support multi-line devices, where a single phone can be registered with multiple SIP accounts from different providers, each with its own credentials and authentication settings.

User mobility features allow credentials to be stored separately from device identity, so users can input their personal information at any compatible device and access their home services and preferences. However, fixed devices registered with the network administrator should use the local device location for emergency calls rather than user-specified locations. These features collectively enable SIP to function as a flexible, user-friendly communications platform.
sections.eli5: A phone should have a web page where you configure it without special software. You should be able to log in with your credentials and use any phone, or have multiple phone numbers on one device.

sections.title: Accessibility, Presence, and International Support
sections.content:
Devices with displays should support presence information showing the availability status of contacts, including busy, do-not-disturb, and call-state indicators. When do-not-disturb is enabled, devices must respond to new calls with a "486 Busy" response. Devices should support interactive text conversation for accessibility, allowing deaf and hard-of-hearing users to communicate via real-time text alongside or instead of voice. Some devices may support buddy lists and instant messaging for richer communication.

International deployment requires that devices support user-selected languages for menus, help text, and labels, and indicate the preferred language to the network. Emergency calling should follow guidelines for emergency response, and devices in regions supporting emergency preparedness should accept the Resource-Priority header to distinguish urgent calls from routine ones. These provisions ensure SIP telephony is accessible and usable worldwide.
sections.eli5: A phone might show whether people are busy, let you type messages instead of talk, and support languages other than English. It should help in emergencies and work in any country.
